newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House approves $85 billion net tax cut.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House approves $85 billion net tax cut.

text.p: The House approved legislation Thursday that would cut taxes by a net $85 billion over five years to give Americans the biggest tax reduction since 1981.

The House voted 253-179 to pass the bill, with 27 Democrats voting for it and one Republican voting against it. The legislation would implement the tax portion of the balanced budget agreement reached between congressional leaders and the White House.
The Clinton administration said it "strongly" opposed the House bill.
The Senate continued debating its version and differences in the two bills must ultimately be ironed out before final legislation can be sent to the president.
Both the House and Senate defeated Democratic alternative tax bills that were offered.
Democrats criticised the Republican bill as giving too big a share of the tax relief to the wealthy.

"Who should be getting the lion's share of the benefit from this tax cut bill?" House Democratic Leader Dick Gephardt of Missouri said. "We want everybody to have a tax cut, we just want the lion's share of it to go to hard working middle income families and families trying to get in the middle class."
Republicans said the bulk of the tax relief would go to the middle class.

"It's unfortunate we have to deal with this economic class warfare rhetoric over and over again," said House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican. "I don't know where these numbers come from that say the rich get richer."
The single biggest piece of the tax cut was a $500-per-child tax credit. The legislation also included tax breaks for college education and expanded Individual Retirement Accounts.
The House bill would cut the capital gains tax rate to 20 percent from the maximum 28 percent for individuals and gradually reduce the rate for corporations to 30 percent from 35 percent.

The legislation would gradually raise the threshold where the estate tax is imposed to $1 million in 2007 from the current $600,000. The House bill would eliminate the ethanol subsidy after it expires at the end of 2000 and raise revenues from airline ticket taxes and passenger fees.
The Senate version amounted to a net $77 billion tax cut over five years, with a pledge from Republican leaders that it will at some point be brought up to the $85 billion mark.
Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle said he would vote for the Republican bill, despite concerns most of its benefits would flow to the wealthiest Americans.
"We don't want the perfect to be the enemy of the good. There are some good things in here," the South Dakota Democrat said.
He said he hoped to work with the White House to improve the measure in coming weeks when House and Senate negotiators work out a final, compromise bill.
House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, said he fully expected those negotiations to yield legislation that President Clinton would sign into law.

"The fact is we have worked with the president. It is our full expectation ... that when the negotiations are done, both of these bills will be signed," Gingrich said referring to tax and spending bills.
